baby-toddler-fruit-and-vegetables-with-y.title: Baby Toddler fruit and vegetables, with yogurt

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit and vegetable puree with yogurt is designed for babies and toddlers. It contains carefully selected fruits, vegetables and natural yogurt, providing a balanced mix of vitamins, minerals and probiotics.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The combination of fruit, vegetable and yogurt helps develop taste preferences in young children.
Yogurt in the product contains live cultures beneficial for gut microbiota.
All ingredients undergo gentle heat treatment that preserves most vitamins.
The product contains no added sugar, artificial colors or flavors.
Packaging is made from safe, reusable material.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Fruits and yogurt provide B1, B2 and B6 vitamins, essential for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C from fruits and probiotics from yogurt help strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Digestive health
items.content: Probiotics in yogurt promote a healthy gut flora, improving digestion.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Yogurt supplies calcium needed for bone and teeth development in children.

items.title: Vision development
items.content: Beta‑carotene from vegetables converts to vitamin A, important for eyesight.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Children with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy should avoid the product.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although no added sugar is present, natural fruit sugars may need to be limited for children at risk of cavities.

items.title: Age restrictions
items.content: The product is recommended for children from 6 months old. Younger infants should be introduced only after consulting a pediatrician.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the puree as a standalone snack or mix into cereals, cottage cheese, or baby desserts. Before serving, gently warm to room temperature if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 2 °C–6 °C. Once opened, consume within 3–5 days. Do not freeze.

content.title: About
content.content: A bagel is a round, ring‑shaped bread made from wheat flour, known for its shiny crust and dense, chewy interior. The dough is briefly boiled before baking, which gives the crust a crisp bite while keeping the crumb moist. Bagels are popular in the United States and Europe and are often topped with seeds, cheese, or filled with various spreads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bagels originated in Eastern European Jewish cuisine.
Boiling the dough before baking creates the distinctive texture that sets bagels apart from ordinary rolls.
Classic New‑York bagels are commonly topped with poppy seeds, sesame seeds, or coarse salt.
In the early 1900s, bagels became a staple street‑food item in New York City.
There are many variations: raisin, cinnamon, cheese, smoked salmon, and even sweet dessert versions.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Wheat flour provides a steady release of energy, helping to keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain bagels supply fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine (B1), niacin (B3) and folate aid metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Bagels provide iron, magnesium and zinc, important for blood health and immunity.

items.title: Low added sugar
items.content: Unlike many sweet pastries, traditional bagels contain little to no added sugar.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Wheat bagels contain gluten and are unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Because the carbohydrates are quickly absorbed, bagels can raise blood‑sugar levels, so diabetics should watch portion size.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Savory bagels often contain added salt, which may be a concern for those with hypertension.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Bagels are dense and calorie‑rich; moderation is key for weight‑management diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bagels are typically sliced, toasted, and spread with cream cheese, avocado, smoked salmon, hummus, or used as a sandwich base. They can also be cubed and fried as croutons for salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep bagels in a paper bag at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, place them in an airtight container in the refrigerator (up to 5 days) or freeze them in a freezer‑safe bag.

content.title: About
content.content: Banana nectar is a sweet non‑alcoholic beverage made from concentrated juice of ripe bananas, diluted with water and sweetened to taste. It has a strong banana aroma, a light golden colour and a smooth, slightly creamy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Banana nectar is a popular base for tropical cocktails and desserts.
Unlike plain banana puree, nectar is pasteurised, which extends its shelf life.
It contains more vitamin B6 than most fruit juices.
Nectars made from different banana varieties can vary in sweetness and aromatic notes.
Banana nectar is often served chilled as a refreshing summer drink.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Potassium helps maintain fluid‑electrolyte balance and supports normal heart function.

items.title: Source of vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C provides antioxidant protection and supports the immune system.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Banana nectar contains virtually no fat, making it a light beverage option.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Small amounts of dietary fibre help promote regular bowel movements.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Many commercial banana nectars are sweetened, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Banana allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to banana products.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The natural acidity can irritate a sensitive stomach.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Certain brands contain additives that may be undesirable for sensitive consumers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink banana nectar chilled, use it in smoothies, cocktails, desserts, or as a base for fruit punches. It can also be mixed into yogurt or oatmeal for a banana flavour boost.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep banana nectar refrigerated after opening, in a sealed container, and consume within 5‑7 days. Protect it from prolonged exposure to sunlight and high temperatures.

cheese-sandwich-american-cheese-on-wheat.title: Cheese Sandwich, American Cheese, on Wheat Bread

content.title: About
content.content: A cheese sandwich with American cheese on wheat bread is a simple and popular snack. The layer of meltable American cheese adds a smooth, creamy flavor, while the whole‑grain wheat bread provides a light crunch and extra fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: American cheese was created in the early 20th century as a way to use leftover dairy solids.
Wheat bread is often chosen for sandwiches because of its softer texture compared to white bread.
Cheese sandwiches are commonly served in U.S. school cafeterias as a quick source of energy.
The combination of cheese and whole‑grain bread improves the bioavailability of some B‑vitamins.
In some countries, a cheese sandwich is considered a traditional breakfast item.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: American cheese provides calcium, which is essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The cheese supplies high‑quality protein needed for muscle repair.

items.title: Fiber from whole‑grain bread
items.content: Wheat bread adds dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both cheese and whole‑grain bread contain B1, B2, and B12 vitamins that aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: The sandwich rapidly replenishes glucose stores, useful for active lifestyles.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: American cheese often contains a lot of salt, which can be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: The saturated fat in cheese may raise cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort after eating.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein can trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Prepare the sandwich by placing a slice of American cheese between two pieces of wheat bread and lightly toasting or grilling until the cheese melts. Optional additions include tomato slices or lettuce for extra flavor and nutrients.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. For longer freshness, keep cheese and bread separate: cheese in its original packaging and bread in a sealed bag to prevent drying.

chicken-fillet-sandwich-grilled-on-wheat.title: Grilled Chicken Fillet Sandwich on Wheat Bun with Cheese

content.title: About
content.content: The grilled chicken fillet sandwich features a tender piece of chicken breast cooked on a grill, placed between a split wheat bun and topped with melted cheese. The sandwich combines juicy chicken, a lightly crisp bun, and creamy cheese, making it a popular choice for a quick lunch or snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Grilling preserves most of the protein and gives the meat a distinctive smoky flavor.
A wheat bun provides slower‑releasing carbohydrates, keeping energy levels steadier than white bread.
Cheese not only adds taste but also boosts calcium and vitamin D content.
Chicken breast is one of the leanest meats, containing minimal saturated fat.
Sandwiches are often served with vegetables like lettuce, tomato, or cucumber, increasing their nutritional value.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken fillet is a rich source of complete protein, essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many meat products, chicken breast contains very little saturated fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: The cheese layer adds calcium, important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Energy from whole‑grain bun
items.content: A wheat bun supplies complex carbohydrates that digest slowly, helping maintain stable blood sugar.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both chicken and whole‑grain bread provide B6 and B12 vitamins, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared sandwiches may contain added salt, especially if processed cheese is used.

items.title: Cross‑contamination risk
items.content: When grilling, avoid contact between raw and cooked meat to prevent foodborne illness.

items.title: Gluten in wheat bun
items.content: Individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should opt for a gluten‑free bun.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the sandwich hot right after grilling, or let it cool slightly. It is commonly served with lettuce, tomato slices, cucumber, or a yogurt‑based sauce. For a lighter option, replace the wheat bun with a whole‑grain or gluten‑free alternative.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the assembled sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. For longer storage, separate the chicken, bun, and cheese, wrapping the cheese tightly in plastic. Reheat the chicken on a grill or in a microwave before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicory (Cichorium intybus) is a perennial plant in the aster family with blue flowers. Both the leaves, which have a pleasant bitterness, and the root, which is roasted and ground, are used as food. The leaves are added to salads and braised, and the roasted root is made into a caffeine-free coffee-like drink. Radicchio, endive, and witloof are also types of chicory.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicory is related to lettuce, dandelion, and artichoke.
Radicchio, endive, and witloof are varieties of chicory.
Roasted and ground chicory root is used as a coffee substitute or additive.
Chicory's blue flowers open in the morning and close by midday.
Chicory root is a source of inulin, which is used in the food industry as a dietary fiber.

items.title: Contains inulin
items.content: Inulin is a prebiotic fiber that feeds beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and helps you feel full.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K plays a role in blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains polyphenols
items.content: The polyphenols in chicory have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Caffeine-free drink
items.content: A drink made from chicory root contains no caffeine.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Chicory can cause allergies, especially in people sensitive to ragweed, mugwort, and other plants in the aster family.

items.title: Bloating
items.content: A large amount of inulin can cause gas and bloating.

items.title: Pregnancy and supplements
items.content: During pregnancy and breastfeeding, large amounts of the root and supplements should be discussed with a doctor.

items.title: Gallstones
items.content: Chicory increases bile flow, so people with gallstones should consult a doctor.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add chicory leaves to salads, or roast, braise, or grill them to soften the bitterness. The root, after roasting and grinding, is used for a drink: brew the powder with hot water or milk, or mix it with coffee. For a less bitter taste, soak the leaves in cold water.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh leaves in the refrigerator, wrapped in a paper towel or in a container, for three to five days. Keep witloof in a dark place, because in light it turns green and bitter. Store dry ground chicory in an airtight jar in a dry place.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-cheese-.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with cheese and meat, made with margarine

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of eggs prepared as an omelet or scrambled eggs, combined with cheese and meat ingredients, fried in margarine. It is popular as a quick breakfast or light dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are an excellent source of complete protein containing all essential amino acids.
Cheese adds calcium and enhances the flavor richness of the dish.
Meat (ham, bacon, or sausage) increases iron and vitamin B12 content.
Margarine is often used instead of butter because of lower cost and longer shelf life.
The dish can be prepared in 5–10 minutes.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Eggs and meat provide high‑quality protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains calcium
items.content: Cheese supplies calcium, which supports bone and dental health.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and meat deliver vitamins B2, B6, and B12 important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Provides iron
items.content: Meat adds heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The dish offers a quick calorie boost, useful for high energy demands.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggs, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Margarine and cheese can contain saturated fats, so people with high cholesterol should consume the dish in moderation.

items.title: Sodium and salt
items.content: Meat additives and cheese often contain salt; excess sodium may raise blood pressure.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish is relatively high in calories, so portion control is advisable for weight‑managed diets.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Beat the eggs, add grated cheese and diced meat. Melt margarine in a pan, pour in the egg mixture, and cook over medium heat, stirring until the desired consistency is reached. Optionally add herbs, spices, or vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The dish is best eaten fresh. If needed, store in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat in a pan or microwave before serving.

fruit-juice-drink-with-high-vitamin-c.title: Fruit Juice Drink with High Vitamin C

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit juice drink is a beverage obtained by pressing fresh fruits and enriched with vitamin C (5333 mg/L). It has a bright aroma, refreshing taste, and vivid colour. The juice can be made from oranges, kiwi, strawberries and other berries rich in vitamin C.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The vitamin C content is ten times the daily recommended intake for an adult.
Minimal heat processing preserves most antioxidants.
Regular consumption supports immunity and speeds recovery from colds.
The drink is often used as a base for marinades, sauces and desserts.

items.title: Immune system support
items.content: Vitamin C enhances the activity of immune cells, helping the body fight infections.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Vitamin C neutralises free radicals, slowing cellular aging processes.

items.title: Improved iron absorption
items.content: Vitamin C increases the bioavailability of plant‑based iron, important for preventing anemia.

items.title: Skin health
items.content: Vitamin C participates in collagen synthesis, promoting skin elasticity and repair.

items.title: Reduced fatigue
items.content: High doses of vitamin C can help lessen feelings of tiredness and boost energy levels.

items.title: Excessive vitamin C intake
items.content: Very high doses may cause gastrointestinal discomfort such as diarrhea.

items.title: Allergy to fruit components
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to specific fruits used in the juice.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Vitamin C can affect the efficacy of certain drugs, for example anticoagulants.

content.title: How to Consume
content.content: Drink the juice chilled, 200‑250 ml per day. It can be added to smoothies, cocktails, used as a base for fruit punches or incorporated into culinary recipes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the drink in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C in a sealed container for up to 5 days. When frozen, it can be kept for up to 3 months in portion‑size containers.

content.title: About
content.content: Popcorn Microwave Plain Light (2987) is a ready‑to‑cook microwave bag containing whole corn kernels without added flavorings or salt. When heated, the kernels pop into light, airy pieces that make a quick snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Popcorn is one of the few corn varieties whose kernels explode when heated due to internal moisture.
Microwave popcorn was introduced in the 1980s and quickly became popular for its convenience.
The light version usually contains less fat and fewer calories than traditional butter popcorn.
Popcorn is a common snack at movie theaters and sporting events because it is fast and easy to prepare.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Light microwave popcorn typically contains 1–3 g of fat per serving, making it less caloric than butter‑flavored versions.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Popcorn is high in dietary fiber, which supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Whole corn kernels provide polyphenols that may help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Popcorn naturally contains no gluten, suitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Moderate glycemic index
items.content: Compared with many snack foods, popcorn has a moderate glycemic index, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Burn risk
items.content: Steam released from the hot bag can cause burns; open the bag carefully, keeping your face away from the steam.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Although marketed as plain, some batches may contain a small amount of salt, which should be considered if you limit sodium.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may be allergic to corn; avoid the product if you have a known corn allergy.

items.title: Possible additives
items.content: Certain versions may include preservatives or flavor enhancers; check the ingredient list if you are sensitive to food additives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Place the bag in the microwave, unfolding it according to the package directions. Cook on high power for 2–3 minutes, stopping when the interval between pops exceeds 2 seconds. Let stand for 30 seconds, then carefully open, stir, and enjoy.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened bag in a cool, dry place away from moisture. After opening, keep the popcorn in an airtight container to prevent moisture absorption, which can cause premature popping.

content.title: About
content.content: The diet chocolate flavored soft drink is a calorie‑free carbonated beverage that uses artificial sweeteners and chocolate flavoring. It retains the characteristic fizz while containing no sugar and virtually no calories, making it popular among weight‑conscious consumers.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first chocolate‑flavored soda hit the US market in the 1970s as an alternative to traditional colas.
Chocolate flavor is usually achieved with a blend of cocoa butter, natural or artificial flavor compounds, and a small amount of caffeine.
Diet versions are commonly sweetened with sucralose, aspartame, or stevia.
The chocolate aroma is strongest when the drink is served cold, so it is typically chilled before consumption.
Some brands add a touch of vitamin B12 to market the drink as an “energy‑boosting” option.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: The absence of sugar and near‑zero calories allow the drink to be enjoyed without contributing to weight gain.

items.title: Sugar‑free
items.content: Suitable for people with diabetes or those limiting glucose intake.

items.title: Caffeine content
items.content: A modest caffeine dose can increase alertness and concentration.

items.title: Antioxidant flavorings
items.content: Certain flavor compounds contain flavonoids that have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Like any carbonated beverage, it helps maintain fluid balance.

items.title: Artificial sweeteners
items.content: Some individuals may experience gastrointestinal discomfort or heightened sensitivity.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The low pH can contribute to dental enamel erosion with frequent consumption.

items.title: Caffeine
items.content: Excess intake may cause insomnia, rapid heartbeat, and anxiety.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Flavorings may contain trace amounts of dairy or soy.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the drink chilled, preferably in a glass or aluminum bottle. It can be used as a base for mocktails, added to protein shakes, or drizzled over desserts such as ice cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, reseal the bottle and consume within 3‑5 days to preserve flavor and carbonation.

content.title: About
content.content: Spinach is a leafy vegetable belonging to the Amaranthaceae family. Fresh spinach cooked with a small amount of oil retains its bright green color, delicate flavor, and nutritional value. It is commonly used in side dishes, salads, and Asian cuisine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Spinach provides more than 20 vitamins and minerals, including vitamin K, vitamin A, and iron.
Oxalate levels decrease with heat treatment, especially when cooked with oil.
In ancient Rome spinach was considered a "food of the gods" for its vivid color and aroma.
Spinach is cultivated in over 70 countries, with the United States, China, and India being the largest producers.
Leaf color can range from light green to deep purple depending on growing conditions.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for normal blood clotting and supports bone health.

items.title: Source of vitamin A and carotenoids
items.content: Beta‑carotene, which converts to vitamin A, supports vision and immunity.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron from spinach contributes to hemoglobin formation and helps prevent anemia.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin protect the eyes from age‑related changes.

items.title: Low‑calorie fiber source
items.content: Fiber improves digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: High oxalate content
items.content: Oxalates may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Possible drug interactions
items.content: Vitamin K can reduce the effectiveness of anticoagulants such as warfarin.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergy to spinach.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spinach cooked with a small amount of oil works well as a side dish, in pastas, omelets, or Asian stir‑fries. Sauté the leaves for 2‑3 minutes until they soften but retain a bright color.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh spinach in the refrigerator in a bag or container with a slight moisture to keep it crisp for up to 5 days. Cooked spinach should be consumed within 2‑3 days, kept in an airtight container.

content.title: About
content.content: Pickled vegetables are a mix of various vegetables (cucumbers, carrots, cauliflower, peppers, etc.) that have been preserved in a brine made of vinegar, salt, spices, and sometimes sugar. The pickling process keeps them crunchy and gives them a characteristic tangy‑sweet flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pickling has been used since ancient times as a way to extend the shelf life of vegetables.
The acidity of the brine (usually 2–3 % acetic acid) inhibits the growth of pathogenic bacteria.
Traditional recipes often include spices such as mustard seeds, dill, coriander, and black pepper.
In many countries pickled vegetables are considered a national dish (e.g., Korean kimchi).
Pickled vegetables can be served cold or hot (e.g., hot pickled cucumbers).

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: Vegetables retain most of their vitamin C, vitamin K, and provitamin A (beta‑carotene) content.

items.title: Source of probiotics
items.content: Fermented pickles (such as sauerkraut) contain beneficial bacteria that support gut microbiota.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Most pickled vegetables are low in calories, making them a good choice for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytochemicals like polyphenols remain in pickled vegetables and help combat free radicals.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: The acidity of the brine stimulates gastric juice production, improving digestion.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Large amounts of salt can raise blood pressure; people with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Acid reflux
items.content: The acidic brine may aggravate heartburn in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some spices (e.g., mustard seeds) can cause allergies.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improper storage above 4 °C can allow growth of harmful bacteria such as Clostridium botulinum.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pickled vegetables can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, sandwiches, sushi rolls, stews, or used as a side dish for meat. Slice them thin for rolls or serve whole on appetizer platters.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated in the original brine in an airtight container. Properly stored, they stay good for 2–3 weeks. Discard if the smell becomes sharp, mold appears, or the brine turns cloudy.
